data.name: A Different Approach To Men's Mental Health
data.description: Explore the barriers men face in seeking mental health care and approaches that make asking for help easier.
data.thumbnail: assets/A Different Approach To Men's Mental Health.jpg
data.html:
A Different Approach To Men’s Mental Health

There is a long history of stigma around mental health. Men often face extra challenges when trying to get the help they need. These barriers can be reduced by using an approach that better meets men’s needs.

Challenges and Barriers

Men may show signs of mental health struggles through behaviors such as:

  • Anger
  • Misusing alcohol or drugs
  • Suicidal ideation or attempts

Society teaches men not to ask for help. They may turn to dangerous behaviors to cope instead of trying to get the help they need.

The Treatment Gap

Men may not want to talk about their mental health or feelings. They will avoid services like counseling or support groups that do not meet their needs. Healthcare providers may not offer other choices due to a lack of knowledge or unfair beliefs about men’s mental health.

How to Close the Gap

Men need mental health care that understands their needs and life experiences. Treatment should help men learn to solve problems and create a safe, supportive place for men to share their feelings.

Workplace and community programs can help men learn about mental health and how to ask for help.

Encouraging Men to Ask For Help

Men are more likely to use mental health services that help them solve problems and find positive ways to move forward. Therapy can be used as a tool for solving problems and growth.

Men who do regular physical anctivity have better mental health. Group exercise programs give men a chance to stay active while building connections with others.

Stress at work can also have an affect on mental health. Work demands and trying to juggle different roles can make things more stressful.

To help men improve their mental health you must remove the barriers to care. This begins with understanding the challenges they face. A treatment approach must meet men’s needs. This helps them feel supported and improves their well-being.

References

  • American Psychiatric Association. (2025, May 1). Move your mind: How daily physical activity boosts brain health and mental well-being. https://www.psychiatry.org/news-room/apa-blogs/daily-physical-activity-boosts-brain-health/
  • Griffith, D. and Jaeger, E. (2024, April 2). Men and mental health: What are we missing? Association of American Medical Colleges. https://www.aamc.org/news/men-and-mental-health-what-are-we-missing
  • McKenzie S., Ramsden, G., Every-Palmer, S., Ahir-Knight, S., and Oliffe, J. (2026). ‘It Puts You at Odds With Society’: Masculinity and Men’s Experiences of Mental Illness Stigma. Qualitative Health Research. doi:10.1177/10497323261450776
